turn_text: Representative Robert Pitinger of North Carolina recently took to the pages of the Wall Street Journal and he referred to the amendment that you sponsored with Congresswoman Loffgren to rein in NSA surveillance as making the mistake of going much too far in protecting privacy. You obviously disagree. So what does your amendment do?

Well, there's been a lot of talk about the metadata, how everybody's phone records are being collected and archived. There's another program that's been referred to as the PRISM program where the government actually collects your content of your emails, your photographs, records your phone calls, your chat sessions. We're talking about content here. That's only if there's reasonable expectation that somebody on the other end is overseas. But in the process of that's a fairly big filter and a lot of stuff gets through, a lot of genuine US persons conversations are being harvested. which is okay, we understand that's gonna happen, but when they query that big database or the haystack as they call it, they should be going in there and looking for terrorist type information because this is under FISA, this is not under the Patriot Act, this is under foreign intelligence regime. But here's the problem. That program has evolved, and they're going in there querying that database with your name, my name, some identifier that's uniquely unique to a US person. And it's basically a phishing expedition without a search warrant, without probable cause. So, all our amendment does, that Zoh, Loffgren, and I offered, is it says you have to have probable cause on a search warrant if you're going to dive into that database and go looking for US person's stuff in there. Now, there's a second part to our amendment. By the way, that's called backdoor searches in the media, that's sort of the name that's evolved. There's another backdoor that's being exploited by the US government that, as the second half of our amendment, seeks to address. Our federal government right now can use its money and its influence to coerce companies to put secret encryption keys or defects into their software that will allow the US government to basically give them backdoor keys, if you will, into US products. The problem with that, just the pragmatic problem, is it's killing our sales of hardware and software overseas in Europe. Now, if you're in Europe, it's a windfall. If you're a manufacturer in Europe, you can say, look, you can be sure if you're buying a German product, we're not putting American backdoor keys in the products. And so it's hurting our competitiveness overseas. So those are the two things that our amendment does. It passed 293 to 123. It's an amendment, but I think it's important to point out that's a veto-proof majority if it were a standalone bill.
